newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Tight pricing turns off Philippine Yankee buyers.
newsitem.headline: Tight pricing turns off Philippine Yankee buyers.

text.p: Tight pricing offered for the Philippine Centrl Bank's maiden yankee bond issue has turned off several potential buyers, senior bankers and bond traders said on Tuesday.
Salomon Brothers, awarded a fresh mandate to underwrite the 30-year and 100-year bond earlier in the day, has begun offering it for a possible launching later in the day in New York.
The 30-year bonds are being offered at 185 basis points above the U.S. long bond, while the 100-year bond is 197.5 bp over.
"We find the spread a bit too tight, considering the 20-year Philippine (Brady exchange bond) is trading at 180 basis points over in the secondary market," a senior trader at a foreign bank said.
"We've turned them down. We're better off buying the 20-year Eurobond on the secondary market," another trader at a large domestic bank told Reuters.
The two bankers said the secondary market for both the 20- and 30-year bonds could be interesting as the price of one would have to correct.
"Something has to give," the senior trader said, adding either the spread of the 20-year bond goes down or the spread of the 30-year goes higher.
Salomon Brothers and the Central Bank both declined to give details of the new mandate, saying that they still needed prior clearance with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
"All I can tell you is that it's a very good spread for us," a beaming Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson told reporters after the bidding.
Bankers said Salomon Brothers had offered a very low price to make up for the problems with the initial issue plans.
The Central Bank revamped its proposed maiden offering last week, disbanding the original Salomon-led underwriting syndicate and calling for new bids by Tuesday morning.
Instead of the "best effort" basis, the underwriting contract was offered to the six original syndicate members on a firm basis, though only five bid.

The volume was also cut from its original $1 billion. While the issuers declined to say how large was the offering, bankers said Salomon was selling $400 million worth of 30-year bonds and $100 million worth of 100 year bonds.
The Philippines had planned to launch the bond on April 15 but eventually pulled out, citing unfavourable market conditions.
Investors had expected a 225 to 230 basis point spread then, but the Central Bank was only willing to pay up to 205 bp.
Squabbling over fees, pricing and timing prompted the Central Bank restart the bidding, a Bank official said.
One trader said the offered spread was the same spread commmitted to the Central Bank. "All Salomon is getting out of the it is its fees," he said.
However, another trader said the offering might still be considered a good buy given the strong economic outlook of the country.
"With the Philipines looking at a possible upgrade into investment grade in a year or two, it will be a good buy," a senior bond trader at a foreign bank said.
